original_question: Characterize the planar n-point sets P with D(P) = O(n/sqrt(log n)), meaning sets that span a near-optimal number of distinct distances up to the currently best known order of magnitude.
target_in_paper: Section 2, Problem 2: "Characterize the near-optimal point sets."
correct_elements: Your draft identifies the correct target class and the correct task: it is about structurally characterizing planar n-point sets whose number of distinct distances is on the paper’s near-optimal scale D(P)=O(n/sqrt(log n)). It also stays focused on the global classification problem, rather than drifting into one of the narrower follow-up problems about many collinear points or points on curves.
missing_details: You should define D(P) explicitly as the number of distinct Euclidean distances determined by pairs of points of P.
You should state the ambient setting explicitly: P is a finite subset of R^2 with |P|=n.
For full paper-faithfulness, it helps to introduce D(n):=min_{|P|=n} D(P), since the paper defines 'near-optimal' relative to the still-unknown asymptotic behavior of D(n).
You should clarify that the condition D(P)=O(n/sqrt(log n)) is asymptotic in n, with an absolute implied constant independent of n.

The phrase 'currently best known order of magnitude' is slightly loose here: in the paper, O(n/sqrt(log n)) is used as a surrogate notion of near-optimality because the true asymptotic of D(n) is not known.
You should make explicit that no extra hypotheses are assumed: no general-position condition, no lattice hypothesis, and no restriction on lines/circles/curves.
The official formulation to match is the concise open problem 'Characterize the near-optimal point sets'; the nearby 'lattice structure' discussion is motivation, not the formal statement itself.
refined_question: Let P ⊂ R^2 be a finite set of n points, and let D(P) denote the number of distinct Euclidean distances determined by pairs of points of P. Write D(n):=min_{|P|=n} D(P). Since the exact asymptotic behavior of D(n) is unknown, call P near-optimal if D(P)=O(n/sqrt(log n)). Characterize the near-optimal point sets.
justification: The draft matches the formal open problem in Section 2. In the introduction, the paper highlights 'characterizing the point sets in R^2 that span a small number of distinct distances' as one of the main challenges. Section 2 then defines near-optimal planar sets by the condition D(P)=O(n/sqrt(log n)) and immediately states Problem 2: 'Characterize the near-optimal point sets.' The adjacent discussion that asks whether every such set 'has lattice structure' only motivates the problem; the later statements about heavy lines and heavy curves are narrower follow-up problems, so they should not replace Problem 2 as the target.
